did_you_know.text: Did you know? The psalm opens with a heading attributing it to David and including the phrase “To the tune of ‘The Doe of the Dawn.’” The text itself indicates that it was intended for the music director.
Did you know? The cry “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” does not describe a refusal to address the Lord. Rather, it is a direct appeal to him amid a sense of distance and distress.
Did you know? The psalmist describes praying continually, without pause: he calls to the Lord by day and by night, yet feels that he is still not answered.

Did you know? Alongside his sense of silence, the psalmist calls the Lord “holy” and recalls that he is enthroned amid Israel’s praises. In this way, he connects his personal distress with the people’s history of faith.
Did you know? The psalmist recalls three things that Israel’s ancestors did: they trusted in the Lord, cried out to him, and were rescued. This memory forms the basis of his personal request.
Did you know? The phrase “a worm and not a man” expresses the psalmist’s profound humiliation. He goes on to describe himself as scorned by humanity and despised by the people.
Did you know? The mockery of the opponents is expressed both in words and in body language: they “hurl insults” and shake their heads.

Did you know? The psalmist describes the Lord as accompanying him from the very beginning of his life: the Lord brought him out of the womb and has been his trust since he was at his mother’s breasts.
Did you know? The enemies are portrayed through animal imagery: many bulls and the mighty bulls of Bashan surround and encircle the psalmist.

Did you know? In the final part of the psalm, the focus broadens from personal distress to a universal vision: all the ends of the earth and all the families of the nations will remember, return to the Lord, and bow down before him.
